scenes.text: Every few days, another serious bug makes the news. A bug that lets someone skip the login. A bug that leaks private data. A bug that hands an attacker your computer.
Sometimes it's Windows. Sometimes Linux. A browser, a database, a cloud service... or a small library that millions of developers depend on.
And the reaction is almost always the same. How did the programmers miss this?
These are professionals. They have code reviews, automated tests, security audits, fuzzing... and the bugs keep coming anyway.
So is it even possible to write complex software without bugs?
Let's start with a number. Imagine a program with just a hundred settings, each of them either on or off.
A hundred simple yes-or-no decisions. How many combinations is that?
Two to the power of a hundred. That's roughly a million trillion trillion.
Now imagine you could test a billion combinations every second. And you started at the Big Bang.
By today, you'd have tested about one combination in three thousand.
And a hundred switches is nothing. A real program has millions of them. So "just test everything" isn't expensive. It's impossible.
And those switches aren't exotic. Take one of the simplest things a program ever does. A user asks for their account by its number. We find it in the database. We send it back.
But what if the user doesn't exist? What if someone sends text instead of a number? Or a negative number? Or an enormous one?
What if this person isn't allowed to see it? What if someone deletes the account at the exact moment we're loading it? What if the same request arrives twice?
Every one of these questions is simple. The problem is how they combine. Each one is another switch.
By the way, if you like videos like this, consider subscribing. It really helps the channel.
And a computer won't sort them out for us. It does exactly what we tell it to. Not what we meant.
That's why we invented programming languages. They let us describe complex things without thinking about every detail.
But some of them take care of less than you'd hope. Take C. It's fast, it's simple, and it gives you enormous control over memory.
So you can write this. We reserve room for sixteen characters. Then we say: copy the input here.
What if the input is five hundred characters long? C won't ask. It just keeps writing past the end.
And what's right after those sixteen characters? Often, something very important.
When a program calls a function, it writes down where to go back once the function is done. A return address. In a classic layout, it sits not far past the end of our buffer.
So an attacker sends an input of exactly the right length. First, their own instructions. Then, at the very end, a new return address... pointing back at those instructions.
The function finishes. The processor looks up where to return... and jumps straight into the attacker's code.
Now it's running their program, with all the permissions of yours. That's what "executing arbitrary code" means.
And the processor didn't do anything wrong. It followed the instructions.
In 1988, a mistake exactly like this let the Morris worm spread across the early internet. And the same trick has been used in attacks ever since.
So newer languages hand part of the job to the compiler. Rust, for example, refuses to build many programs that could misuse memory.
The programmer says: but I know exactly what I'm doing! And the compiler says: that's what everyone says.
And it's right to be suspicious. Microsoft and Google's Chrome team have both reported that around seventy percent of the security bugs they've studied come from memory safety problems.
But a program can be perfectly memory-safe and still completely wrong.
Imagine a user logs in. Their password is checked correctly. Nothing crashes. No memory is corrupted.
And then the program shows them somebody else's data. Because the permission check was written slightly wrong.
No language can catch that on its own. The language doesn't know what the program was supposed to do. Only we know that.
So back to testing. A test can tell you: for this input, I got this result.
It can't tell you: the program is right for every input. And we've already seen why we can't try them all.
In 1970, the computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra put it in one sentence. Testing can show the presence of bugs, but never their absence.
Fine. So instead of testing, why not write a program that checks other programs and proves they're correct? Feed it any code, and it tells you whether that code does what it should.
That question was answered before the first real computer was even built. In 1936, Alan Turing proved that a program like that cannot exist.
Not that nobody has built it yet. That it can't exist at all.
He showed that no program can decide, for every other program, whether it will ever stop running.
And in 1953, Henry Rice went further. The same is true for every non-trivial question about what a program actually does.
Is it secure? Does it leak data? Does it give the right answer? There is no general method that settles that for every program.
So is bug-free software impossible? Not quite. For one specific program, you can sometimes prove it correct, with enormous effort.
In 2009, a team in Australia proved that a small operating system kernel, called seL4, does exactly what its specification says.
It was under ten thousand lines of code. Building the kernel took about two person-years. Proving it correct took about twenty. A modern web browser has tens of millions of lines.
And even that proof has a catch. It shows the program matches its specification. It can't show that the specification is what we actually wanted.
And the specification is written by people. So the question comes back to us.

And it isn't only our own code. A programmer today builds on frameworks, libraries and hundreds of dependencies. Every layer saves us enormous amounts of work. But every layer is something we have to understand... or at least trust.
Which means you don't have to write a bug to have one in your software. You can simply install it.
Then add the pressure. Nobody wants a perfect product in ten years. They want a working one next month. And a break-in that never happened is very hard to show in a presentation.
And here's the strangest part. Our tools keep getting better. Safer languages, fuzzing, bug bounties...
And yet the number of known vulnerabilities keeps growing. In 2024 alone, around forty thousand got an official number.
Partly because we're also writing vastly more software than ever. It's like making every road safer... while building millions of times more roads.
So are programmers bad at their jobs? No. We've been asking them for something that no general method can guarantee.
So maybe "how do we write software without bugs?" is the wrong question.
The better question is: how do we build systems that stay safe even when the software has bugs?
And that's exactly where security is heading. It doesn't say: never make a mistake. It says: assume you already have.
Remember that return address? Today, the system guards it. It shuffles where things sit in memory. And it refuses to run instructions hidden in data.
The bug in our C code is still there. It's just much harder to turn into an attack.
And the same idea is everywhere. Sandboxes, limited permissions, isolated processes, encryption, backups, monitoring... layer after layer, so that one bug doesn't become a disaster.
And it has a very practical consequence. If bugs are inevitable, fixing them isn't optional.
The software you're using today may well contain a vulnerability nobody has found yet.
And when someone does, the update is the difference between "a vulnerability was discovered" and "we were hacked".
The same goes for the systems we build. Old libraries and unsupported platforms don't get safer by being ignored. They turn into technical debt.
And why that debt has to be paid off is what my video "It Still Works. So Why Upgrade It?" is about.
Because in software, "it still works" and "it's still safe" are two very different things.
